| [0010](./0010/) | core | draft | major | not-started | 2026-07-29 — D24-D28 recorded; D13's keying half and D14's role REVERSED; OQ11-OQ15 filed; OQ7 reframed. The trigger was a scenario the entry could not serve: a generic `backup` resource and trait defined in catalog_opm with NO transformer of its own, fulfilled by a k8up provider catalog the platform installs. Under D13 the demand key carries the catalog_opm build the MODULE compiled against and the supply key carries the build the PROVIDER compiled against — `materialize/pull.go:23` loads each catalog as its own root, so the provider's own cue.mod fixes it — and the two must be EQUAL. D14's breadth cannot repair it: subscribing to every catalog_opm build supplies every build's own transformers, and a provider-fulfilled primitive has none, so coverage is the set of catalog_opm versions the provider's release history happened to pin. Every catalog_opm release breaks the contract until the provider re-releases AND every module is rebuilt to match — an N x M lockstep between two independently-released catalogs. D24 SPLITS THE KEY BY ROLE: resources, traits and blueprints key on a per-primitive `apiVersion` (`path/name@v1`), a contract major moved only when that primitive's shape breaks and independent of both the catalog's module major and its release SemVer; transformers keep the full build SemVer, which is what keeps materialize/index.go's distinct-versions-distinct-keys invariant true and is the mechanism that made D4 unworkable. The split follows the demand direction — a module demands resources and traits and never demands a transformer. D4's catalog-major keying was rejected separately and on its own grounds: one version namespace per catalog means breaking one trait needs a catalog major bump, so in practice it never happens and the promise becomes unenforceable, whereas a per-primitive version gives a catalog a cheap legitimate way to break one contract on purpose — and admits two apiVersions of one primitive shipping SIDE BY SIDE, the migration path SemVer keys cannot express. D25 adds `apiVersion` as an authored field (the one identity value NOT derivable from identity/identity.cue, which is why it is a field rather than an interpolation) and renames `version` to `catalogVersion`; `moduleVersion` was rejected because `module` already means three things in OPM and would read as the field D2 deleted. D27 states the promise the key now rests on: inside one apiVersion, add never remove, a new field must be optional or defaulted, and an existing field's default is IMMUTABLE. D26 is the finding that makes any of it work, and it was not predicted: experiments/02-primitive-closedness-skew measured that with catalogVersion an ordinary metadata field, EVERY build skew fails on `metadata.catalogVersion: conflicting values` whether or not the shapes agree — major keys exist so two builds can meet at one key and the provenance field stops them meeting at all. Provenance is therefore excluded from the operands BEFORE unification; the mechanism is deliberately open (OQ12), and cutting at `spec` instead was measured and rejected because closedness is inherited from the enclosing definition, so an inline spec body silently drops a field the module set while a named schema definition catches it — and catalog_opm ships both styles. The same experiment measured the property the whole model rests on: a provider older than the contract fails LOUDLY (`spec.backup.retention: field not allowed`) exactly when the module uses what the provider lacks, and passes when it does not. D28 makes an unresolved demand an error — every declared resource required, traits opt-out — on the finding that `plan.Missing` has no production consumer at all (populated match.go:130, read only by tests) and there is no UnhandledResources counterpart, so a component with a container and an unsupplied backup renders successfully today with no backup. WHAT THIS COSTS is recorded rather than glossed: D13's reproducibility argument survives and RELOCATES — the key no longer pins the transformer build, so the platform's subscription must, and it currently floats (filter.go:43-47 highest-stable, Resolved in-memory only). That is OQ11 and it is the one place the new model is worse until answered. OQ15 supersedes OQ7's framing: breadth loses its job but stays structurally available, and if kept it acquires a failure D14 never had — several builds of one transformer in one contract bucket, all satisfying the predicate, all rendering. | Module and Catalog Identity |
| [0011](./0011/) | cli | draft | minor | not-started | 2026-07-29 — D9 recorded and OQ7 filed, both consequences of enhancement 0010's D24-D28. D9 gives `opm catalog publish` a COMPATIBILITY GATE: for each primitive, pull the last published build shipping that name at that apiVersion and refuse a non-additive change, per 0010 D27. It is not redundant with the consumer-side check, and the measurement says why — 0010's experiments/02 found that the match rung catches a removed field and a narrowed type but NOT a changed default, because two builds disagreeing on a default unify to a non-concrete value, so the match passes and the render fails later on an incomplete value naming a field rather than a build. The one violation the consumer cannot catch is the one that silently moves output. Two bounds are stated rather than assumed: subsumption is transitive so the immediate predecessor secures the whole history by induction, but only while every build passes the gate, and D11 in 0010 records that `cue mod publish` keeps working — whether that gap gets a read-side counterpart is 0010 OQ13. The implementation is deliberately unspecified because `cue.Value.Subsume`'s behaviour across two builds with closedness and defaults in play is UNMEASURED; 0010's experiment already carries the four builds a correct gate must classify, so sequencing that measurement before specifying the command is a graduation gate — a gate that cannot be built as described sends 0010 D27 back to publisher discipline. OQ7 asks who owns a catalog name. The provider-catalog scenario introduces exactly the actor D5's owner-scoping exists for, and D5 gives modules an owner segment while leaving catalogs flat — where the argument applies with MORE force, since a catalog's name is the permanent prefix of every FQN every module matches on and 0010 D24 makes contract keys outlive any single build. A third party publishing a k8up provider catalog today either gets OPM to host `opmodel.dev/catalogs/k8up`, which reads as endorsement and makes OPM the arbiter D5 wanted to avoid, or publishes under their own domain and is unresolvable for anyone who has not edited CUE_REGISTRY, which D5's own rationale rules out. | Module and Catalog Publishing |

| [0013](./0013/) | cross-cutting | draft | - | not-started | 2026-07-27 — Design revised on review: D10 supersedes D1, D11 supersedes D4, D12 amends D9, and OQ1 is closed. D1 had removed the `#Secret` contract type AND the disjunction inside it, when only the routing metadata needed to move to the attribute — leaving the deployer no slot in which to say "this Secret already exists", and forcing the handle-plus-context-map machinery of D4 to compensate. D10 restores `#Secret` narrowed to `#SecretLiteral | #SecretRef`, so the ATTRIBUTE carries routing (author intent, static, in the published module) and the TYPE carries fulfilment (deployer choice, per environment, type-checked by CUE). D11 replaces handle substitution with resolve-in-place: the kernel rewrites every secret to its `#SecretRef` form, so both arms converge before render, a transformer reads two fields from one branch, and the whole handle format, the `#TransformerContext` addition, the `owned` flag and the output scanner are all deleted. Three properties fall out that the first draft lacked: instance files for supplied secrets do not change at all, plaintext in the render is structurally unrepresentable rather than stripped, and a secret interpolated into a rendered string fails at plain `cue vet` at authoring time. Experiment 02 rebuilt as `02-resolve-in-place` and re-run: all five claims held, and its Go content hash agrees with the CUE one in examples.cue. OQ2 opened — whether the arm rewrite survives the real kernel build path — and is now the sole blocker to acceptance. | Attribute-Declared Secret Fields |
| [0014](./0014/) | cli | draft | none | not-started | 2026-07-29 — Drafted. 0006 shipped the handoff that moves an instance's manager to the operator; nothing moves its definition out of the cluster, so a CLI-first user who now wants GitOps hand-assembles four YAML documents per instance from a `kubectl get -o yaml` dump. Three decisions came from the user on the day: the exported unit is the CR plus its apply envelope rather than a bare CR (D1), export refuses to write unless the published module reproduces `status.lastAppliedRenderDigest` (D2, reusing handoff's gate chain and `VerificationDigest`), and `spec.values` is written verbatim with a warning rather than redacted or refused, because OPM cannot yet identify which values are secret (D3). D4 records the live CR as the sole input. Two findings from reading the code shaped the design. `ApplySpec` (cli/internal/inventory/store.go:119) writes only `spec.module`, `spec.owner`, and `spec.values`, so every CLI-written CR lacks `spec.serviceAccountName` and `spec.prune` — meaning a dump-and-strip export applies under the controller's own identity and orphans its workloads on delete, a behaviour difference invisible in the YAML. And the render-bearing / apply-bearing partition resolves the tension that finding creates: the fields the digest gate verifies are copied untouched, while the fields governing apply identity and deletion sit outside the render digest and can be completed without weakening the guarantee, provided every completion is reported. The partition is enforced in schemas/target.cue rather than asserted in prose. Six open questions; OQ4 (field-manager collision when Flux's kustomize-controller applies over fields owned by opm-cli and the operator) is the load-bearing one and is gated on a runnable experiment, because it decides whether the adoption is as quiet as D2's guarantee implies. | Export a Deployed Instance as GitOps Manifests |

## Status legend

- **draft** — initial design, actively being written
- **accepted** — design agreed upon, ready for implementation
- **implemented** — design has been realized in code
- **superseded** — replaced by a newer enhancement (see `superseded_by` in the entry's config.yaml)
